name: Wayoro
confidence_why: Nogueira 2011 and 2019, the only full descriptions of Wayoro, mark stress in their transcriptions but never state where it falls, and Moore and Galucio 1994 report no evidence of contrastive stress while leaving the tone question open, so nothing on record disagrees with leaving the placement undetermined, though only two independent fieldwork lineages exist.

catalog_quote: [Nogueira 2011, p. 39] Nos dados abaixo, a vogal média-alta posterior [o] ocorreu opcionalmente realizada como vogal alta posterior [u], em sílabas não acentuadas: (2) [o] ~ [u] em contexto átono [ko.i."|o] ~ [ku.i."|o] “mamão” [o."|È] ~ [u."|È] “gato-do-mato” [o."Bi] ~ [u."Bi] “1s.pé” [tõ.nda."|ap}] ~ [tu).nda."|ap}] “mururé” [pa.ko."|i] ~ [pa.ku."|i] “lua” ... [Nogueira 2019, p. 25] Pronomes em posição inicial — posição em que são claramente pronunciados com acento próprio — não desencadeiam lenição, mesmo que configurem um ambiente intervocálico. ... Nossa hipótese é que tais pronomes tenham acento próprio, na posição inicial, e, por isso, não formem uma unidade fonológica com a palavra seguinte.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both cited passages are verbatim at the stated pages in the held PDFs/txts (2011 p.39; 2019 p.25). (2) Deciding source: a 2011 USP MA thesis whose phonology chapter is segmental only, backed by the 2019 PhD; these are the principal descriptions of Wayoro (Glottolog lists nothing else) and neither states where stress falls, so not determinable is a faithful reading. (3) I downloaded and read six further open items (Moore & Galucio 1994; Galucio & Nogueira 2012; Nogueira 2013, 2014/15, 2015; Nikulin & Andrade 2020): none gives a placement rule; Moore & Galucio 1994 p.122 adds only that stress is non-contrastive in Ayuru, and Nikulin & Andrade 2020 treat Wayoró as having no described stress. The one document that could change the classification is Nogueira's unpublished 2010 qualifying report on segmental and suprasegmental phonology (author request only). (4) The record's own observation

sources.citation: Moore, Denny & Ana Vilacy Galucio. 1994. Reconstruction of Proto-Tupari consonants and vowels. In: Margaret Langdon (ed.), Survey of California and Other Indian Languages, Report 8, pp. 119-137. Berkeley. (Ayuru = Wayoro is one of the four languages)
sources.quote: "There is no evidence of contrastive stress in the four languages. The question of tone is unresolved. In Ayuru there are two pitch levels in ascending sequences, but at least three or four levels in descending sequences." (scanned text, checked in context)
sources.locator: p.122 (p.5), phonology overview before the consonant inventory

sources.citation: Nikulin, Andrey & Rafael Andrade. 2020. The rise and fall of approximants in the Tuparian languages. Journal of Language Relationship 18(3-4): 284-319.
sources.quote: "The acute accent denotes stress in Tuparí and Akuntsú and high tone in Makurap" — no stress marked or discussed for Wayoró (data from Nogueira 2011, 2015, 2019); conclusion lists 'the reconstruction of the Proto-Tuparian prosody (which should minimally account for the contrastive stress in Tuparí and Akuntsú and for the tonal patterns of Makurap)' as future work.

sources.quote: Gives the vowel inventory and the /ɛ-/ → [a-] dissimilation; no statement about stress.

sources.note: The only work on Wayoro with a suprasegmental component in its title; the 2011 MA explicitly omitted suprasegmental information (fn.15), so this report is the one place a stated stress rule could exist and could move the record from not determinable to a coded (probably final-stress) value.
